->To the Holy Child<-

->**J E S U S.**<-

You whose supreme Majesty,
Great God, hides itself in a child,
Triumphant in the highest heavens,
And among us, weakness itself!
The Bliss of Saints, yet you shed tears;
You who uphold the earth and the sea,
Are born of a fruitful Virgin,
And though filled with delights, you sink under sorrows! <note>This stanza reflects the "theology of paradox" common in the Baroque period, contrasting Christ's divine power with his human vulnerability.</note>

Word <note>original: "Verbe," referring to the *Logos* or the Second Person of the Trinity</note> extinguished, silent speech,
Immense, yet equal to our children!
Infinite, held within the womb <note>original: "flans" (literally "sides" or "flanks," a poetic term for the womb)</note>
Of her whom you yourself created!
Who, to set us free, enters into our bonds,
And to return us to your Father,
Comes into this foreign land <note>In Christian tradition, the "foreign land" refers to the earthly world as a place of exile from Heaven.</note>,
To take our poverty, and give us your riches!

G 4 <margin>G 4 is a signature mark used by early printers to help binders assemble the book pages in the correct order.</margin> King <margin>This is a "catchword," the first word of the following page, included to ensure the text flows correctly during printing.</margin>

### To the Holy Infant Jesus

->Through these words, wound the souls,<- <note>original: "bleſſez les ames"; in 17th-century devotional language, to "wound a soul" meant to pierce it with a deep, longing love for the divine.</note>

<meta>This page contains the legal "Privilege" or royal license for the book, a standard feature of 17th-century French publishing. It provides historical context for the work's publication and legal standing.</meta>

*Extract of the King’s Privilege.*

**B**y the grace and Privilege of the King, given at Versailles on the 10th day of July, 1687, signed by the King in his Council by De-Lamet, and sealed with the Great Seal of Yellow Wax, permission is granted to ANTOINE BRIASSON, Bookseller at Lyon, to have a Book printed entitled, *the Song of Songs of Solomon, interpreted according to the mystical sense, and the true representation of interior states,* <note>This title refers to the mystical commentary by Madame Guyon, a central figure in the Quietist movement.</note> and this for the time and space of six consecutive years, counting from the day that the printing is completed for the first time; with prohibitions to all persons of whatever quality and condition they may be, against printing it or having it printed, without the consent of the said Briasson or his legal successors; under penalty of a fine <note>original: "amande"—an archaic spelling of "amende."</note> of two thousand livres, the confiscation of the counterfeit copies, and all costs, damages, and interests, as is contained more at length in the said letters of privilege.

*Registered in the Book of the Community*
*of Booksellers and Printers*
*of Paris, the 21st of July*
1687. signed,

I. B. COIGNARD, <term>Syndic</term>. <note>A Syndic was a representative or official of a professional guild—in this case, the guild governing the book trade.</note>

Printing completed for the first time
the 15th of September 1687.

*The copies have been provided.* <note>This refers to the "legal deposit" requirement, where copies of a new book had to be provided to official libraries or authorities.</note>

AP.

<summary>This page presents the official royal license granted to the bookseller Antoine Briasson to publish a mystical commentary on the Song of Songs. It establishes a six-year copyright and sets heavy fines for any unauthorized reproductions, demonstrating the controlled nature of the 17th-century French book trade.</summary>

<meta>This page contains the preliminary "Approbations" (official ecclesiastical approvals) for the publication, dated August 1687. These documents certify that the work aligns with Church doctrine and carries the endorsement of high-ranking clergy in Lyon.</meta>

**APPROBATIONS.**

**T**he Book of Canticles <note>Also known as the Song of Songs or the Song of Solomon</note> is so mysterious that it belongs only to those who possess the spirit, the capacity, and the piety of St. Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a mystic whose 86 sermons on this biblical book are considered the definitive spiritual commentary of the Middle Ages</note> to penetrate and explain it; and history bears witness that persons highly accomplished in doctrine have not dared to undertake the unfolding of these hidden meanings and these sacred enigmas; this is why I am seized with astonishment when I consider that the Author of this Book has explained the Song in a manner so easy, so beautiful, and so edifying. He is indebted for this to the communications of the Holy Spirit, which blows where it wills <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 3:8</note>; I give this testimony in his favor, at Lyon this 20th of August, the feast day of St. Bernard, in the year 1687.

**COHADE.**

***

**I**, the undersigned Priest, Doctor of Canon Law, Bachelor of the Sorbonne, General Syndic of the Clergy of Lyon, Custodian of the Parish of the Holy Cross, and Lieutenant in the Ordinary and Metropolitan Officialty <term>Officialty: The ecclesiastical court of a diocese, responsible for judicial and administrative matters</term> of this Diocese, attest that this explanation of the Book of Canticles is all the more to be esteemed because the subject matter is very delicate to treat—
G 6 <note>This "G 6" is a printer's signature mark, used by early modern bookbinders to keep the pages in the correct order.</note>

The union of the powers <term>powers: the faculties of the soul, traditionally categorized in Christian mysticism as the memory, the understanding, and the will</term> is that by which God unites Himself to the soul quite superficially: it is more a matter of touching her <note>In the original French, the soul ("l'âme") is feminine, often depicted as the "bride" of the Divine.</note> than uniting with her. She is nevertheless united to the Trinity of Persons, according to the different effects which are attributed to them: but always as to distinct persons, and through mediate operation; the operation serving here as both means and end, in that the soul rests in this union that she experiences, not believing that it is necessary to go further. 

This union occurs in order within each of the powers of the soul; and it is perceived sometimes in one, or two of them, according to God’s design; and at other times, in all three together. This constitutes the application of the soul to the Holy Trinity, as to distinct Persons. 

When the union is in the understanding alone, it is the union of pure knowledge, and it is attributed to the Word <note>original: "Verbe," the second person of the Trinity, or the Logos</note>, as a distinct person. When the union is in the memory, which occurs through an absorption of the soul in God, and a profound forgetting of created things; it is attributed to the Father, as a distinct person. And when it makes itself felt in the will alone, through a loving enjoyment,
without <note>This page ends mid-sentence; the text continues on the following page.</note>

...munication of the <term>Word</term><note>Original: "le Verbe." In mystical theology, this refers to Christ as the Eternal Logos communicating directly to the spirit.</note> to the Soul, I say that it is necessary that this soul must have arrived in God alone, and that she be established there by essential union and by spiritual marriage, before this divine communication is made to her; just as the fruits and the productions of marriage only take place after it has been consummated.

This is more real than can be expressed; and since God here possesses the entire soul without interruption, this is what constitutes the difference between union with God Himself and other unions. In unions with created beings, the object can only be possessed for moments, because creatures are outside of us. But the enjoyment of God is permanent and lasting, because it is within ourselves; and since God is our ultimate end, the soul can ceaselessly flow into Him, as into its destination and its center, and there be mingled and transformed, never to depart again. It must further be observed that God, in creating us, gave us a **participation** <term>Participation: In a theological sense, this refers to the way created beings "share" in the qualities of God (like life, reason, or goodness) without being identical to Him.</term> in His being, designed to be reunited with Him; and at the same time, an inclination toward this reunion. One can be united without being mingled. This is the union of the powers <note>In mystical theology, the "powers" (puissances) refer to the faculties of the soul: the intellect, the will, and the memory.</note>: But mingling is the essential union, and this union is entirely complete, occurring from the whole into the whole. Now, this occurs when the soul loses its own consistency, so as to subsist only in God: this must be understood mystically, by the loss of all self-ownership <term>proprieté: the spiritual ego's tendency to claim its virtues, experiences, and "self" as its own property rather than God's</term>, and by a loving and perfect flowing back <note>original: "récoulement"</note> of the soul into God. Rather, it is like a drop of water that loses its perceptible consistency when it is placed in a vat of wine, where it is perceptibly changed into wine; although its being and its matter always remain distinct from it: and an Angel could, if God willed it, perform the separation. In the same way...

154  **The Song of Songs**

They are so fragrant that, through their charming scent, they attract those souls fortunate enough to perceive them; they are also like a precious balm that heals all internal <note>original: "intérieures"</note> wounds. If such is already the case in these first approaches, what delights will there be in the nuptial kiss, the "kiss of the mouth"? <note>In mystical theology, the "kiss of the mouth" represents the highest state of spiritual union between the soul and God, moving beyond mere "approaches" to total intimacy.</note>

The ultimate goal is proposed at the very beginning of this Song; it stands as the reward and the perfect consummation for the Bride <note>In this tradition of commentary, the "Bride" is understood to be the individual human soul.</note>. This is because it is natural for the vision and desire of the goal to precede the selection of the means to reach it. Thereafter, the means of reaching this state are described in order, beginning with spiritual childhood <term>Spiritual Childhood: A stage of the interior life marked by humility, simplicity, and total dependence on God, often viewed as the necessary starting point for spiritual growth.</term>. It is the vision of this very same goal that moved the Bride to first ask for "the kiss of the mouth"—even though this is the final gift to be granted to her, and one she will only receive after she has earned it through many trials and labors.

### On Solomon, Chap. 1. v. 6. 167

And because this wandering comes from the fact that one does not sufficiently consult the maxims and the examples of Jesus Christ, and that one does not address Him enough through prayer to obtain what He alone can grant us: this Beloved <note>The "Amante" or "Lover" represents the human soul or the Church in mystical tradition</note>, already well-instructed, asks Him with much insistence for the understanding of His word, with which He feeds souls, and the faithfulness to follow His examples; knowing that this alone, sustained by grace, can prevent her from wandering. One relies too much on created means <note>External rituals or human-made methods</note>, however pious they may be: God alone (a) can teach us to do His will: because He alone is our God. 

She also asks the Word <note>The "Verbe," referring to the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</note> to lead her to His Father, since He is the Way that must lead there. The bosom of His Father being the place where He rests in the noon <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:7, "where you rest your flock at noon," interpreted here as the height of divine glory</note> of His glory, and in the full light of eternity: she wishes to lose herself in God with Jesus His son, to be hidden there, and to rest there forever. 

And although she does not say it so clearly, she makes it known well enough by what she says afterward: *So that I may no longer be wandering here and there, as I have been, I will be there in all security, I will no longer be able to be deceived, and what is even more, I will no longer be able to sin.*

My Beloved, this Lover continues, is to me like a cluster of henna; she explains herself only halfway. The Lover compares her Beloved to the good scent and the rare virtue of the balm, and to the pleasantness and strength of wine, to express through these figures that whoever, through the inner taste for God, has learned to take delight in him, can no longer find pleasure in any other thing: And that as soon as one seeks any other delights, one loses the divine ones.

### [Of] Solomon, Chap. 1. v. 16. [Page] 181

When the Bridegroom <note>In mystical tradition, the "Bridegroom" represents Christ or the Divine.</note>, hidden in the depths and the center of the soul (as has been said), takes pleasure in sending from this Sanctuary where he dwells certain outpourings of his **sensible graces** <term>sensible graces: Spiritual feelings or "consolations" that can be perceived by the human senses and emotions, often given to encourage beginners in their faith.</term>, which produce in the exterior of the Bride <note>The "Bride" represents the individual human soul.</note> a multitude of different virtues, which are like so many beautiful flowers with which she sees herself adorned: surprised and charmed as she is—or perhaps through a lack of experience—she believes that her interior edifice is almost finished.

"The roof-coverings," she says, "are already placed; the rafters, which are the practice of exterior virtues, are made of cedar wood. It seems to me that they have a pleasant fragrance for me, and that I can practice them with as much strength as ease."

The regulation of the senses appears to her to be in an order as precise as well-crafted paneling made of exquisite wood. But, oh *Beloved*, this only appears so to you because this bed is flowered; and because the sweet, agreeable, and pleasant state that you feel within makes you believe that you have acquired everything for the outside. But consider that the paneling is of cypress; that the cypress signifies death, and that what you see so beautiful and so adorned is prepared only for death <note>original: "ciprés ſignifie la mort". In Christian symbolism, the cypress is often associated with mourning and cemeteries; here, it refers to the "death of the self" or the ego required for deeper spiritual union.</note>.

182 *The Song of Songs*

# CHAPTER II.

Verse 1. I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys. <note>original Latin: "Ego flos campi, & lilium convallium."</note>

*I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys.*

O God, you gently rebuke your Spouse <note>In mystical literature, the "Spouse" or "Bride" represents the human soul or the Church in its relationship with God.</note>, because she wished to rest so soon in a bed adorned with flowers, before having rested, as you did, upon the sorrowful bed of the Cross. I am, you say, myself the flower of the field; a flower that you will not gather in the rest of the bed, but in the field of combat, of labor, and of suffering. I am the lily of the valleys, which grows only in <term>annihilated souls</term> <note>The term "annihilation" (anéantissement) refers to a central concept in 17th-century French spirituality where the soul's self-will is completely surrendered to God.</note>. Thus, if you wish for me to pull you from your own earth, and for me to take life in you, you must be in the state of ultimate self-emptying: and if you wish to find me, you must enter into the struggle and into suffering.

# From Solomon, Chapter 2, verses 12–13. Page 199.

...me, compared to the vine, be pruned, for the time of pruning has arrived. <note>In the Song of Solomon 2:12, the Hebrew word *zamir* can mean both "pruning" and "singing." While many modern Bibles translate this as "the season of singing," this commentator follows the Latin Vulgate tradition (*tempus putationis*), emphasizing the spiritual "pruning" or discipline of the soul.</note> It is not enough that the winter has passed—that is to say, that the soul has been stripped of all external things—it is also necessary that it be pruned. It must lose all that is superfluous, all that is of its own growth and its own industry; and it must also lose all those branches that would want to spread out toward the outside, in order to remain perfectly centered within itself and its God.

->**Verse 13. The fig tree has brought forth its early figs, and the blossoming vines have yielded their scent.** <note>original Latin: "Ficus protulit grossos suos, et vineae florentes dederunt odorem suum."</note><-

The fig tree has produced its early figs <note>The French text uses "fausses figues" (false figs), translating the Latin *grossos*. These are the small, green, unripened figs that appear early in the season, symbolizing the first movements of grace in the soul that are not yet mature fruit.</note>, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance.

**THERE** the springtime is eternal, and it lengthens and loses itself in a most perfect and most delightful summer. The soul, having left the winter of its coldness and its sins, enters into this spiritual springtime where it begins to produce the flowers of all the virtues. These flowers are still tender, but they exhale a most sweet fragrance before the Lord. It is in this state that the soul is truly "flowering," no longer seeking its own satisfaction, but only the pleasure of its Beloved. This fragrance is the "odor of life" which attracts the Divine Spouse to come and rest in the garden of the soul. <term>Odor of life</term> <note>A reference to the "aroma of Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:16), signifying a soul that is pleasing to God through its inner transformation.</note>

The virtue of simplicity, so highly recommended in the Scriptures, <note>Likely a reference to Matthew 10:16: "be wise as serpents and simple as doves."</note> makes us act toward God incessantly, without hesitation; directly, without reflection; <term>reflection: in this spiritual context, "reflection" refers to the mind's tendency to turn back on itself to monitor its own progress or motives, which was seen as a distraction from pure love.</term> and sovereignly, without a multiplicity of designs, motives, or practices: but solely to please God. And even when simplicity is perfected, one usually acts this way without thinking about it. To act simply with one's neighbor is to act with naturalness, without affectation; with sincerity, without disguise; and with freedom, without constraint. These are the eyes and the heart of the dove which char— <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "charment" (charm/delight) or "charactérisent" (characterize).</note>

# [Commentary] on Solomon, Chapter 4, verses 3, 4. 229

Since the will of this Beloved <note>The "Amante" or female lover represents the human soul in mystical tradition.</note> loves only her God, and all her affections are for Him; the Bridegroom compares her to a **scarlet-dyed ribbon**, which signifies the affections reunited into a single will, which is all charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *caritas*, the highest form of divine love.</note> and all love; all the powers of this will being gathered together in their divine object.

<meta>This page is the preface (Avertissement) to a collection of the works of Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection (c. 1614–1691). It follows a likely discussion of the efforts made to gather his scattered writings after his death.</meta>

->**PREFACE**<-

...as many as could be found of those letters he had written with his own hand, among which was found a manuscript entitled *Spiritual Maxims, or Means for Acquiring the Presence of God*. These maxims and these letters are so edifying, so full of <term>unction</term><note>original: "onction"; in 17th-century spiritual writing, this refers to a quality of speech or text that is deeply moving and inspired by the Holy Spirit, possessing a "heart-melting" grace.</note>, and were found to be in such excellent taste by those who had the comfort of reading them, that they did not wish to be the only ones to benefit from them. They desired that they be printed, judging rightly that they would be very useful to souls striving for perfection through the practice of the presence of God. And because nothing is more eloquent, nor better persuades one toward the practice of good than a good example, it was believed that to make this little work complete, it would be appropriate to present at the beginning a brief summary of the Author's life. In this biography, one will see such a perfect consistency between his actions and his words that it will be easy to recognize that he spoke only from his own experience.

<meta>This page serves as the "Avertissement" or Foreword to the text, likely "The Practice of the Presence of God" by Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection (Laurent de la Résurrection). It introduces the universal appeal of the work for all social and religious classes.</meta>

->N O T I C E.<-

All Christians will find here something for
their edification; those individuals involved
in the high society of the world will see how
much they deceive themselves by seeking
peace and happiness in the false glitter
of temporal greatness <note>original: "grandeur temporelles," referring to worldly power, status, or wealth that exists only in time, as opposed to eternal spiritual riches.</note>. People
of goodwill will find here the means to
encourage themselves to persevere in the practice
of virtue. Religious persons <term>Religious: In this historical context, "Religious" refers specifically to those who have taken formal vows in a monastic order, such as monks, nuns, or friars.</term>,
and especially those who
are not tasked with the salvation of souls <note>This likely refers to "lay brothers" or those whose duties were domestic (cooking, cleaning) rather than clerical or ministerial.</note>,
will be able to benefit more than others,
since they will see one of their own
Brothers, occupied like them with
outward tasks, and who in the midst of
the most distracting <note>original: "embarrassantes," implying duties that are cluttered, busy, or physically demanding, which might otherwise hinder prayer.</note> occupations,
knew so well how to reconcile action with
contemplation, that in the span of
more than forty years he
almost never turned away from the presence
of God, as will be seen more

**I**t is a constant truth in Scripture, that the arm of God is not shortened <note>original: "le bras de Dieu n'eſt point racourcy" — a reference to Isaiah 59:1, meaning God's power to intervene and save remains as strong as ever.</note>; His mercy being unable to be exhausted by our miseries, the power of His grace is no less great today than it was at the birth of the Church. This habit was so natural to him that, as he explained himself in one of his letters and in what he wrote elsewhere, he spent the last forty years of his life in a constant practice of the presence of God—or rather, to use his own terms, in a silent and familiar conversation with Him.

A fellow monk, whom he felt compelled to answer, asked him one day what method he had used to acquire this habit of the presence of God, the practice of which was so easy and continuous for him. He replied with his usual simplicity: "From my entry into religious life, I looked upon God as the goal and the end of all the thoughts and affections of my soul. At the start of my novitiate, during the hours set aside for prayer <note>original: *l'oraison*. In this context, it refers to "mental prayer" or silent contemplation rather than recited litanies.</note>, I occupied myself with convincing myself of the truth of this Divine Being, more by the light of faith than by the labor of meditation and discourse <note>original: *discours*. This refers to "discursive prayer," an intellectual method of reasoning through religious truths, which Lawrence moved away from in favor of simple intuition.</note>. By this short and certain way, I advanced in the knowledge of this lovable Object <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "Object" refers to the focus of one's devotion—here, God Himself.</note>, with whom I formed the resolution to remain always. Thus, completely filled as I was with the greatness of this infinite Being, I went to ren— <note>The text cuts off mid-word at the bottom of the page, likely "rendre" (to render) or "rencontrer" (to meet).</note>

He maintained that to make this practice easier and to form a habit of it, one needed only courage and good will; a truth he proved much better by his actions than by his words. For it was observed in his conduct, while he performed the duty of a cook <note>Brother Lawrence served as a cook for the Discalced Carmelite priory in Paris for several decades despite having a foot injury from his previous life as a soldier.</note>, that at the height of his constant work, and in the midst of the most distracting tasks <term>distracting; original French: *dissipans*</term> <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "dissipation" referred to anything that pulls the mind away from spiritual focus or inward peace.</note>, he kept his mind focused on God. Although his duties were large and arduous, often performing alone the tasks that two people were accustomed to doing, he was never seen acting with frantic haste; rather, he acted with a proper moderation. He gave each thing the time it required, always maintaining his modest and tranquil air, working without slowness and without hurry, remaining in a steady equality of mind and in an unalterable peace.

He performed this office with all possible charity for the space of thirty years or thereabouts, until Providence ordered otherwise; a large ulcer developed on his leg, which obliged his Superiors to employ him in a gentler duty. This change gave him more leisure to adore God.

Finally, we cannot give greater testimony to God of our faithfulness than by renouncing and scorning the creature <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "the creature" refers to any created thing, person, or worldly distraction, as opposed to God the Creator.</note> a thousand and a thousand times over, in order to enjoy the Creator for a single moment.

I do not intend by this to oblige you to leave the external world <note>French: *l'exterieur*, referring to outward activities, social duties, and sensory experiences.</note> forever; that is impossible; but prudence, which is the mother of virtues, must serve as your rule. I say, however, that it is a common error among spiritual persons not to leave the external from time to time to worship God within themselves, and to enjoy His divine presence in peace for a few short moments. This digression has been long; I believed the subject required this full explanation; let us return to our practices.

*On the union of the soul with God.*

THERE are three kinds of unions: the first, habitual; the second, virtual; and the third, actual.
   1. Habitual union is when one is united to God solely through grace. <note>In 17th-century theology, "habitual" refers to a stable state or disposition of the soul, such as being in a "state of grace," rather than a repeated habit.</note>
   2. Virtual union is when, upon beginning an action by which one has united oneself to God, one remains united to him by the virtue <note>The word "virtue" here carries the Latin sense of *virtus*, meaning power or efficacy. The original intention carries through the duration of the task.</note> of that action for as long as it lasts.
   3. Actual union is the most perfect, and as spiritual as it is, it makes its movement felt because the soul is not asleep as in the other unions, but finds itself powerfully stirred. Its operation is more vivid than that of fire, and more luminous than a Sun that is not obscured by a cloud; nevertheless, one can be deceived in this feeling, which is not a simple expression of the heart, such as saying, "My God, I love you with all my heart," or other similar words; but it is a sweet, peaceful <term>inexpressible something</term> <note>Original: "je ne sçai quoy." This was a popular term in French mystical writing to describe a spiritual experience that defies literal description.</note> of the soul,

*On the Presence of God.*

1. The presence of God is an application of our spirit to God, or a remembrance of God present, which can be achieved either through the imagination or through the understanding <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "understanding" refers to the intellectual faculty of the soul, as opposed to the "imagination" which uses mental images.</note>.

But I will say, for the consolation of those who wish to embrace this holy practice, that He usually gives it to souls who prepare themselves for it; and if He does not give it, one can at least, with the help of His ordinary graces, acquire through the practice of the presence of God a manner and a state of <term>Prayer<note>original: "Oraison." This term specifically refers to "mental prayer" or "interior prayer," an internal conversation with God that goes beyond reciting standard vocal prayers.</note></term> that closely approaches this simple gaze.

I cannot understand how religious persons <note>In the 17th century, "religious persons" specifically referred to those living under monastic vows, such as monks or nuns.</note> can live contentedly without the practice of the presence of God; for my part, I keep myself retired with Him in the depth and center of my soul as much as I can, and when I am thus with Him, I fear nothing; but the slightest turning away is a hell to me.

This exercise does not kill the body; it is, however, appropriate to deprive it from time to time, and even often, of several small innocent and lawful consolations; for God does not permit a soul that wishes to be entirely His to take other consolations than with Him; this is more than reasonable.

I do not say that for this reason one must constrain oneself excessively; no, one must serve God in a holy liberty; one must work faithfully, without trouble or anxiety, recalling our spirit gently and quietly to God as many times as we find it distracted.

It is nonetheless necessary to place all one's confidence in God, to rid oneself of all other cares, and even of a great number of particular devotions, <note>Brother Lawrence often advised simplifying one's prayer life by focusing on God's presence rather than reciting numerous specific sets of prayers.</note> altho— <note>The text ends mid-word with "quoy-", likely intended to be "quoy-que" (although).</note>

### IV. LETTER
*To Madame... N...*

**M**ADAME,
I pity you very much. If you could leave the care of your affairs to Monsieur and Madame... N... and occupy yourself with nothing more than praying to God, you would be making a masterstroke; <note>original: "coup d'état." In this context, Lawrence is not speaking of a political overthrow, but rather a "decisive move" or a "brilliant stroke" for the benefit of her soul.</note> He does not ask much of us: a little remembrance from time to time, a little act of adoration, sometimes asking Him for His grace, at other times offering Him your pains, and at others thanking Him for the favors He has granted you, and which He grants you in the midst of your labors. Console yourself with Him as often as you possibly can; during your meals and your conversations, lift up your heart to Him occasionally; the slightest little remembrance will always be most pleasing to Him. One does not need to cry out loud for this; He is closer to us than we think.

It is not necessary to be always in the Church to be with God; we can make of our heart an Oratory <term>Oratory: A private room or space set aside for prayer and devotion.</term>, into which we may withdraw from time to time to converse with Him there gently, humbly, and lovingly— <note>The original French text breaks off mid-word: "amoureu-" (amoureusement).</note>

V. LETTER

*To the Reverend Father .. N ..* <note>The "N" serves as a placeholder to keep the recipient's identity anonymous, a common practice in 17th-century published correspondence.</note>

My Reverend Father,
   Since I do not find my way of life described in books—though I am not at all troubled by this—nevertheless, for greater assurance, I would be very glad to know your thoughts regarding the state in which I find myself.
   A few days ago, in a private conversation with a pious person, they told me that the spiritual life was a life of grace, which begins with servile fear <term>servile fear: a stage of faith driven by the fear of punishment or Hell, rather than by love</term>, increases through the hope of eternal life, and is perfected by pure love; and that each of these stages has various degrees by which one finally arrives at this blessed perfection.
   I have not followed these methods at all; on the contrary, I do not know by what instinct they frightened me at first. This was the reason why, upon entering the religious life <note>original: "entrée en Religion"; this refers to his entry into the Discalced Carmelite order as a lay brother</note>, I made the resolution to give myself entirely to God as atonement for my sins, and to renounce for His love everything that was not Him.

...has committed every kind of crime against his King; touched by a heartfelt regret, I declare to him all my wickedness <term>malices: in this context, refers to one's sins, faults, or inherent fallen nature</term>, I ask his forgiveness, and I abandon myself into his hands to do with me as he pleases. ### XIII. L E T T R E.
#### To the Reverend Mother, N. <note>The "N." is a placeholder used in 17th-century printing to protect the anonymity of the recipient, likely a nun or Mother Superior of a religious community.</note>

MY Good Mother,

If we were well accustomed to the <term>practice of the presence of God</term> <note>This refers to the spiritual discipline of maintaining a constant, silent awareness of and conversation with God throughout the day, regardless of one's tasks.</note>, all bodily illnesses would seem light to us. God often allows us to suffer a little to purify our soul and to compel us to remain with Him. I cannot understand how a soul who is with God, and who wants only Him, could be capable of distress; I even have enough experience of this to have no doubt.

### XIV. LETTER.
### To the same person.

**MY Good Mother,**

It pains me to see you suffer for so long; what softens the compassion I feel for your pains is that I am persuaded they are proofs of the love God has for you; look at them from this perspective, and they will be easy for you to bear; my thought is that you should give up all human remedies, <note>In the late 17th century, medical treatments often involved painful bloodletting or ineffective tonics. <meta>This page serves as the official ecclesiastical endorsement (Approbation) for the work "A Short and Easy Method of Prayer" by Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Motte-Guyon (commonly known as Madame Guyon). This endorsement was crucial for the book's legal publication in 17th-century France.</meta>

->APPROBATION.<-

I, the undersigned Priest, Doctor of Canon Law <note>Original: "Docteur en droit Canon"</note>, Bachelor of the Sorbonne, Syndic General of the Clergy of Lyon, Custodian of Sainte Croix, and Lieutenant in the Ordinary and Metropolitan Officiality <term>Officiality: The ecclesiastical court of a bishop that handled legal and disciplinary matters</term> of this Diocese, have read the Book titled: *Short and Easy Method of Prayer.* <note>Original title: *Moyen court & facile de faire Oraiſon*</note>. It appears that the person who composed this Book is perfectly instructed in the blessed and necessary exercise of Prayer <note>The French "Oraiſon" refers specifically to "mental prayer" or interior, contemplative communication with God, rather than the mere recitation of set prayers.</note>: she knows all its secrets and all its mysteries; she has tasted its sweetness; she has known its utility, and she marks the paths and the means in this book in a manner so holy, so easy, and so clear, that I judge that this book—among so many others that have treated this divine subject, which can never be exhausted—will nonetheless have its own distinction and utility. At Lyon, this 25th of May, 1686.

TERRASSON. <note>André Terrasson was a prominent theologian and preacher in Lyon, known for his support of spiritual writings.</note>

# A SHORT AND VERY EASY METHOD
# OF PRAYER,

*Which all can practice*
*very easily, and by that*
*means arrive in a short*
*time at a high perfection.*

____________________

## §. I.

*All can practice Prayer.*

[Decorative initial T] All are suited for Prayer <note>original: "Oraison." While it translates to "prayer," the author specifically means "mental prayer" or "contemplation"—a silent, internal focus on God rather than the recitation of standard liturgical prayers.</note>, and it is a terrible misfortune that almost everyone gets it into their head that they are not called to Prayer. We are all called to Prayer, just as we are all called to salvation. Prayer is nothing else than the application of the heart to God and the interior exercise of love. St. Paul commands us to pray without ceasing <note>A reference to the biblical exhortation in 1 Thessalonians 5:17.</note>. Our
A 7                                 Lord— <note>The text ends mid-word: "Seigneur" (Lord).</note>

<summary>This opening page argues that silent, heart-centered prayer is a universal duty and privilege for all Christians, not just a select few. It defines prayer simply as the internal exercise of love toward God.</summary>
<keywords>Madame Guyon, mental prayer, Oraison, spiritual perfection, universal calling, interior life</keywords>

--- Page 264 ---
2       *Short & Very Easy Method*       §. I.

The Lord says: *I say it to all of you, watch and pray.* <note>original: "Je vous le dis à tous, veillez & priez." A reference to Mark 13:37.</note> Everyone, therefore, can practice <term>Prayer</term><note>The author uses the word "Oraison," which in this context refers to "mental prayer" or "prayer of the heart"—a silent, internal communion with God rather than the recitation of set formulas.</note>, and everyone must do so. 

But I admit that not everyone is capable of <term>Meditation</term><note>In 17th-century spirituality, "Meditation" usually meant a structured intellectual exercise using the imagination and reason to think about religious truths. The author is arguing that while this "head-work" is hard, her method of "heart-work" is for everyone.</note>, and very few are suited for it. Furthermore, it is not this kind of Prayer that God asks for, nor is it what is desired for you, my very dear brothers—whoever you may be—who wish to be saved. 

Come, all of you, to practice Prayer; you must live by Prayer, just as you must live by love. *I advise you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may be enriched.* <note>original: "Je vous conſeille d'acheter de moy de l'or éprouvé au feu..." This cites Revelation 3:18 (though the text mistakenly cites verse 8).</note> It is very easy for you to have it, more so than you could ever imagine. 

*Come, all of you who are thirsty, to these living waters, and do not waste your time digging broken cisterns that can hold no water.* <note>original: "Venez vous tous qui avez ſoif à ces eaux vives..." This cites Jeremiah 2:13.</note> Come, hungry hearts who find nothing to satisfy you, and you shall be fully filled. Come, poor afflicted ones who are overwhelmed by sorrows and <term>distress</term><note>The original French "ennuis" carried a much stronger meaning in the 1600s than "boredom"; it signified deep mental anguish or weariness of soul.</note>, and you shall be comforted. §. II.
The Method of Mental Prayer.

There are two means to introduce souls into <term>Mental Prayer</term><note>The original French is "Oraiſon," which refers to internal, silent prayer and heart-to-heart communion with God, as opposed to simply reciting set prayers.</note>, which one can and must use for some time. One is Meditation. The other is meditative reading.

Meditative reading is nothing other than taking some powerful truths regarding both <term>speculative</term><note>Theoretical or abstract theological concepts.</note> and <term>practical</term><note>Matters of conduct, virtue, and daily living.</note> matters; preferring the latter to the former, and reading in this manner.

You shall take your truth, whatever you wish to choose, and then read two or three lines of it, in order to digest and taste them, trying to draw out the essence <note>original: "le suc," literally "the juice."</note> and keeping yourself fixed on the passage you are reading as long as you find "flavor" <note>original: "goût," referring to spiritual satisfaction or insight.</note> there, not moving further until that passage has become tasteless to you.

After that, you must take up as much again, and do the same, not reading more...

### ->§. II. *On the practice of Prayer.* 7<-

This practice leads us to plunge ourselves deeply into our own interior, gathering all our senses within and preventing them from scattering outside. This is a powerful method from the very beginning for ridding oneself of a multitude of distractions and for distancing oneself from external objects in order to draw near to God. He can only be found in the depths of our being and in our "center," which is the <term>Holy of Holies</term><note>The author uses the Latin "Sancta-Sanctorum," referring to the innermost sanctuary of the Tabernacle or Temple where God's presence dwelt.</note> where He resides. ### §. 5. *On Practicing Prayer.* 15

...never finish Prayer, without one remaining for some time at the end in a respectful silence. It is also of great consequence that the soul goes to Prayer with courage, that it brings there a pure and disinterested love <note>The author refers to "amour pur," a key concept in 17th-century French spirituality meaning love for God for His own sake, without seeking personal reward or spiritual "feel-good" experiences.</note>: That it goes there not so much to obtain something from God, as to please him and do his will. Are His apparent withdrawals followed by loving caresses? <note>The author refers to the "Divine Absence," a common experience in contemplative prayer where God seems to vanish after a period of spiritual sweetness.</note> One believes then that it is a greater fidelity, and that it shows one's love more, to seek Him with mental effort and by force of action, or that doing so will soon make Him return.

### §. 8. *On making Prayer.* 21

Give yourself to God first for this very thing, and give yourself to Him as a sacrifice; you will see that when the Cross <note>In this spiritual context, the "Cross" refers to the personal trials, hardships, or emotional suffering a person must endure in their life.</note> arrives, it will no longer be so heavy, because you will have willed it. ...by another way. The purely natural reason is that it is the soul that gives strength and vigor to the senses, just as it is the senses that provoke and stir the passions. A dead person no longer has feeling or passion because of the separation that has occurred between the soul and the senses. It is in those things that the soul spreads itself the most; being applied directly to austerity <note>The author refers to "austerities" as physical acts of penance, such as fasting or manual labor, intended to discipline the body.</note> and external matters, it is entirely turned in that direction. This life of the senses stirs and provokes passion rather than extinguishing it. THE Lord *is in his holy Temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.* <note>original: "Le Seigneur est dans son saint Temple, que toute la terre demeure en silence devant lui." — Habakkuk 2:20</note> [ Habakkuk 2:20 ] The reason why interior silence is so necessary is that, since the <term>Word|The author uses "The Word" (French: le Verbe) to refer to Christ as the Logos, the eternal communication of God.</term> is the eternal and essential word, there must be, in order for him to be received in the soul, a disposition that bears some relation to what he is. Does Jesus Christ not assure us that the *Kingdom of God is within us? (Luke ch. 17. v. 21.)* This Kingdom is understood in two ways. The first is when God is so completely Master of us that nothing resists Him any longer; then our interior is truly His Kingdom. The other way is that by possessing God, who is the sovereign Good, we possess the Kingdom of God, which is the height of happiness and the purpose for which we were created, as it is said, *to serve God is to reign.* <note>original: "servir à Dieu, c'est regner." This is a traditional Christian maxim suggesting that true freedom and power are found in submission to the Divine.</note> The purpose for which we were created is to enjoy God even in this life, yet people do not think of it.

The soul then feels that it acts freely and sweetly: though strongly and infallibly.

To properly clarify this point, which is the difficulty for most spiritual seekers <note>original: "spirituels"</note>, for lack of understanding it; one must know that there are passing and distinct acts, and continuous acts; direct acts, and reflective acts <note>A "direct act" is focused entirely on God, while a "reflective act" is when the soul looks back at itself to see what it is doing.</note>. Not everyone can perform the first kind, and not everyone is in a state to perform the others. And the first acts <insert>passing and distinct</insert> must be performed by persons who are turned away. They must turn themselves back by an action that is distinct, and which is more or less strong, according to how far the turning away was distant; so that when the wandering is slight, one of the simplest acts suffices.

§. 24. *On how to pray.* 77

...of discursive prayer <note>original: "l’Oraison discursive." This refers to prayer using the intellect, imagination, and reasoning, typical of beginners.</note>, or even of active contemplation—when viewed as an end in itself rather than a preparation for passive contemplation—are living exercises through which we cannot see God; that is to say, we cannot be united to Him. Everything that comes from man and his own industry <term>industry: the deliberate effort or work of the human mind and will</term>, however noble and elevated it may be, must—I say—all die.

Saint John reports that *there was a great silence in Heaven.* (*Revelation, ch. 8, verse 1.*)

Heaven represents the depth <note>original: "le fonds." A mystical term referring to the innermost part of the soul where God dwells.</note> and the center of the soul, where everything must be in silence when the Majesty of God appears there. All that comes from one's own efforts and from self-ownership <term>self-ownership (propriété): the ego's attachment to its own works, virtues, and will, which prevents total surrender to God</term> must be destroyed. Nothing is opposed to God but this self-ownership, for all the malignity of man resides in this self-interest, as if in the very source of his malice. 

Consequently, the more a soul loses its self-ownership, the purer it becomes. What would be a defect in a soul still living for itself is no longer so, because of the purity and innocence the soul has acquired once it has lost those personal attachments that caused the dissimilarity between God and the soul.

There can be no union because of dissimilarity; since to unite two things, they must be in a proportionate <term>rest</term> <note>original: "repos." This refers to a state of stillness or "quietude" where the soul's own frantic activities cease to allow God to act.</note>.

It is for this reason that the soul reaches divine union only through the rest of its will: and it cannot be united to God unless it is in a central rest, and in the purity of its creation. To purify the soul, God makes use of **Wisdom**, just as one makes use of fire to purify **Gold**. It is certain that gold can only be purified by fire, which gradually consumes everything that is earthly and foreign, and separates it from the gold. It is not enough for the gold to be put to use that the earth is changed into gold: it is further necessary that the fire melts and dissolves it, to draw from its substance everything that remains of the foreign and the earthly; and this gold is put so many, many times into the fire, that it loses all impurity, and any capacity to be further purified.

# NOTICE

It has been thought proper to join to this small work the Letter of a famous Doctor <note>In this context, "Doctor" refers to a highly learned theologian, likely a Doctor of the Church or a significant spiritual authority.</note> and a very great Servant of God. This was done as much to support the maxims <note>original: "maximes"; here meaning fundamental spiritual principles or rules of conduct.</note> contained in this Book with his testimony, as to provide more thorough instruction regarding the manner in which one must enter into the <term>Prayer of Simplicity</term> <note>A form of contemplative prayer, also called the "prayer of rest" or "prayer of faith," where the person remains in a state of quiet, loving attention to God without active reasoning or many words.</note>, and how to persevere in it.

This Letter was composed in Spanish and printed in Madrid from its original manuscript in the year 1657. It was then translated into Italian and printed in Rome, and subsequently rendered into French and printed in Paris. Thus, three great nations have granted it—each in its own language and through its own ecclesiastical tribunals—the approval that it deserves.

In such a way that after having once abandoned yourself to the divine will, and having once placed yourself in the Faith of God present in all things; try to continue this act, and to maintain yourself in it without ceasing. Even if you should spend many hours in this Prayer, even if you should pass the nights there until the break of day, do not trouble yourself with new acts, but continue that of faith and love which you made from the beginning, when you totally abandoned yourself into the hands of our Lord.

*of St. Francis de Sales.* 117

Therefore, what one must do to live in pure and complete hope in God is that as often as distinct forms and images <note>In the context of contemplative prayer, "forms and images" refer to mental distractions or specific intellectual concepts that can pull the mind away from a direct, wordless focus on God.</note> present themselves, without pausing upon them, one suddenly turns the soul to God—empty, and always with loving affection. "I have," he adds, "eaten my honeycomb <note>original: 'raion de miel'</note>." ### 266 *The Song of Songs*

**T**he cheeks of the Bridegroom represent the two parts of his Soul, the superior and the inferior <note>In mystical theology, the "superior" part refers to the highest point of the soul capable of divine union, while the "inferior" part relates to the senses and reason.</note>, which are in such an admirable order that nothing more could be desired; and which give off an inconceivable fragrance. And as the cheeks are joined to the head, so this noble and beautiful Soul is joined to the Divinity. The garden beds <term>carreaux: flowerbeds or raised garden plots</term> full of aromatic plants signify the powers and the interior senses of his holy Humanity, which are all in perfect order. It is certainly a skilled perfumer who has made the choice and who has arranged them so well, since it is the Holy Spirit who has given such a beautiful order to the entirety of the interior and exterior of JESUS CHRIST. His lips are very well compared to lilies: but these are red lilies, which are common in Syria, and of a rare beauty <note>Original: "lis rouges." Likely referring to the *Lilium chalcedonicum* or the Scarlet Martagon, which were known in the Levant and symbolize the blood of Christ.</note>. What lips can be more crimson, more fragrant, and more beautiful than those which pour out words of Spirit and of life, and the knowledge of eternal life? From these same lips drips an excellent myrrh: since the doctrine of JESUS CHRIST leads to repentance, to the mortification of passions, and to continual renunciation <note>Myrrh was traditionally used for embalming and signifies the "bitterness" of self-denial and the death of the ego.</note>.

# CHAPTER VI.

*Verse 1. My Beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of aromatic spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.* <note>original Latin: "Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum ad areolam aromatum, ut pascatur in hortis, & lilia colligat."</note>

*My Beloved has gone down into his garden, even to the flowerbed of aromatic plants, to feed in these places of delight, and to gather lilies there.*

O fortunate Lover, after having searched so much for your Beloved, you finally hear news of him! You had said so much that you would hold him so well, and that you would never let him go; yet, you have let him go further than ever. "Alas," she says, "I was reckless; I did not consider that it did not depend on me to keep him, but that it is up to him to give himself, and to withdraw as he pleases: that I should desire nothing but his will, and be indifferent to his goings and his comings." I confess that my love was <term>self-interested</term> <note>The term "interessé" here refers to a common theme in 17th-century French mysticism regarding "disinterested love"—the idea that one should love God for Himself alone, not for the spiritual "sweetness" or pleasure one receives from His presence.</note>, though I did not know it: I preferred his own pleasure, the pleasure that I had—

*Concerning Solomon, Chapter 6, verse 4*     281

To know at what time the **spiritual marriage** takes place: this is easy to see from what has been previously said. The **betrothals**, or mutual promises, take place in the <term>union of the powers</term> <note>In 17th-century mystical theology, the "powers" or faculties of the soul are the intellect, memory, and will. Their union signifies a state where all these human faculties are perfectly aligned with God's will.</note>; when the Soul gives herself entirely to her God, and her God gives himself entirely to her, with the intention of admitting her to His union; this is an agreement and a reciprocal promise. 

But alas, how much road there is still to travel, and how much to suffer, before this so-desired union is granted and consummated! The **marriage** occurs when the Soul finds herself dead and expired <note>This "death" refers to the mystical death of the self-will and ego, rather than physical death.</note> in the arms of the Bridegroom, who, seeing her better disposed, receives her into His union. 

But the **consummation of the marriage** only occurs when the Soul is so melted, <term>annihilated</term> <note>A key term in mystical writing: the total stripping away of the ego so that the person no longer acts from their own desires, but God acts through them.</note>, and divested of self-ownership, that she can, without reservation, flow entirely into her God. Then takes place this marvelous mingling of the creature with her Creator, which reduces them to a unity, so to speak, though with an infinite disproportion: such as that of a drop of water with the sea. In this state, although the drop has become the sea, it is nevertheless always a little droplet, even though it is proportioned in its quality as water with the whole sea, and fit to be mixed,

               N 3

# Concerning Solomon, Chapter 7, Verses 6–7. 303

GOD, looking upon His Spouse and seeing His own perfections within her, as if in a mirror <note>original: "miroir" and "glace"</note> that reflects them to Him with total fidelity, allows Himself to be enraptured within Himself by the beauty He contemplates in His Spouse. And He says to her: "O my most beloved, how beautiful you are in my beauty, and how beautiful my beauty is in you! You are all my delight, just as I am the delight of my Father. ...portray <note>The source text begins with the fragment "traire," likely the conclusion of the word "portraire" (to portray or depict).</note> you as a beautiful palm tree; you are never straighter than when you are most heavily laden. The female palm tree has two qualities: one is to be even straighter when it is more burdened with fruit; the other is to produce no fruit except in the shadow of its male palm. <note>Early modern natural history often claimed that certain plants, like the palm, had "male" and "female" versions that needed to be planted near each other to bear fruit—a concept frequently used by mystical writers to describe the relationship between the Soul and God.</note> Thus, this beautiful Soul has two qualities: one is never to bend toward herself <note>Meaning she avoids the sin of pride or self-interest.</note> because of any grace she has received from God; the other is to produce not the smallest action by herself, however tiny it may be, but to perform them all in the shadow of her Bridegroom <note>A standard mystical term for Christ.</note>, who causes her to perform each one in its proper time. The breasts are very well compared to clusters of grapes. Grapes have this unique quality: although they are full of liquid, it is not for themselves; instead, the grape gives what it contains to the one who presses it. This Soul is of the same kind: the more she is pressed and oppressed by persecution, the more she shares herself and is beneficent even toward those who do her harm.

THE BRIDE can no longer fear anything: because everything has become God to her, and she finds him equally in all things. ->On Solomon, Chapter 8, verse 4. 317<-

**JUST** as there are three kinds of interior sleeps, so the Bridegroom adjures <note>To command or appeal to someone earnestly, often under oath.</note> three times, at different times, that no one wake his Beloved. The first is in the union of the powers <note>In mystical theology, the "powers" or "faculties" are the intellect, memory, and will.</note>, where she experiences a sleep of violent ecstasy, which flows heavily into the senses. He prays then that she not be awakened: because this sleep is then seasonable, in that it helps to detach the senses from their objects, to which they were impurely attached, and thereby to purify them.

The second is the sleep of death, where she expires in the arms of love. He does not want her to be awakened from it either, until she awakens herself by the effect of the almighty voice of God, who calls her from the tomb of death to a spiritual resurrection. 

The third is the sleep of rest in God, permanent and lasting; it is a rest of ecstasy, but of a gentle and continuous ecstasy, which no longer causes alteration to the senses: the Soul having passed into her God, by the happy departure from herself. It is a rest from which she will never be diverted. He does not want his Lovers <note>The original French "Amantes" is feminine, referring to the souls who love God.</note> to be troubled, nor contradicted in any of their rests: but that they be left to him;

### On Solomon, Chapter 8, Verse 14 [page] 333

This is, therefore, what the Bridegroom <note>In the tradition of mystical commentary, the "Bridegroom" is understood to be Christ, and the "Bride" is the individual Soul or the Church.</note> desires of her: that she speaks to him with both her heart and her mouth, and that she also speaks to others on his behalf.

**Verse 14. Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle, and like a young stag, upon the mountains of spices.** <note>original Latin: "Fuge dilecte mi, & afſimilare capreæ, hinnuloque cervorum ſuper montes aromatum."</note>

*Flee, my Beloved, and be like the gazelle, and the young stag, upon the mountains of spices.*

The Soul, who no longer has any interest other than that of her Bridegroom—neither for herself, nor for any other creature—and who can desire nothing but his glory, seeing something that dishonors him, says to him: "Flee, O my Bridegroom! Depart from these places, which offer you nothing but a foul odor. Go to those Souls who are like mountains of spices, raised high above the corrupt and spoiled vapors caused by the malice of the age <note>The "malice of the age" (French: malice du siècle) is a common 17th-century term for the moral corruption and distractions of the worldly life.</note>. They are mountains of spices because of the scent of the exquisite virtues that you yourself have placed within them."

<summary>This page interprets the final verse of the Song of Solomon as an act of pure love where the Soul, seeking only God's glory, invites the Bridegroom to leave the corruption of the world for the "spices" of virtuous hearts.</summary>
<keywords>Song of Solomon, Bridegroom, Christ, Mysticism, Virtue, Allegory, Spices, 17th Century Spirituality</keywords>

This must be the effect of the deepest annihilation.

Although in this state she is more fit than ever to help Souls, and she serves with extreme care those whom her Spouse directs to her; she is nevertheless incapable of desiring to help others, and can only even do so by a particular order of providence.

442 *The Character*

I have believed it would be useful to show in his person an excellent model of solid piety, in a time when almost everyone places virtue where it is not, and takes false paths to reach it.

It will be Brother Lawrence himself who speaks; I will give you even his own words from the conversations <note>original: "entretiens." These "Conversations" became the most famous part of the collected works of Brother Lawrence.</note> I had with him, which I wrote down as soon as I had left him. No one paints the Saints better than they do themselves. The *Confessions* and the *Letters* of St. Augustine provide a far more natural portrait of him than anything else one could say otherwise; thus, nothing will make the servant of God—whose virtues I have to propose to you—better known than what he said himself in the simplicity of his heart.

The virtue of Brother Lawrence did not make him unsociable <term>sauvage: in this 17th-century context, it implies being withdrawn, wild, or gruffly unapproachable due to religious austerity</term>; he had an open welcome, which inspired confidence and made one feel at once that they could reveal everything to him, and that they had found a friend. For his part, when he knew those with whom he was dealing, he spoke with freedom and showed great kindness. What he said was simple, but always apt and full of good sense. Beneath a rough exterior <note>original: "exterieur groſſier." As a lay brother who spent his life in the monastery kitchen and repairing sandals, Lawrence would have had the calloused hands and plain speech of a laborer, which the author contrasts with his deep inner wisdom.</note> one discovered a wisdom

### 456 The Character <note>Original: *Les Mœurs*. In the 17th century, this term referred to a person’s conduct, habits, and moral character.</note>

...everything else was suspect to him. His great sense, and the light he drew from the **simplicity of his faith**, protected him from all the pitfalls encountered in the path of the spirit—pitfalls against which so many souls today are shipwrecked by surrendering to a love of novelty, to their own imagination, to curiosity, and to purely human ways of behaving.

Nothing is easier than to avoid these dangers when one seeks only God. In matters of Religion, everything that appears new ought to be suspect. This virtue, so necessary, is not among those things that are perfected by the passage of time; on the contrary, it possessed all its perfection at its origin. Jesus Christ taught his Church everything that was necessary for it, either by Himself or by the **Holy Spirit** <note>Original: *S. Esprit* (Saint Esprit).</note>, speaking through the Apostles; and it is to that source that one must return when one wishes to find safety.

458          **The Manners** <note>The French title *Les Mœurs* refers to the conduct, character, or moral customs of the subject.</note>
Let us leave it at that; the Holy Religious <note>A "Religious" is a person bound by monastic vows, in this case, Brother Lawrence.</note> followed it exactly, and provides us in his person an excellent model of the path that leads to God without wandering.

Prepared by such a life, and following such a secure conduct, he saw death appear without distress. His patience had been very great throughout the entire course of his life, but it grew even more as he approached his end. He never seemed to have a moment of sorrow even during the greatest violence of his illness. Joy appeared not only on his face, but also in his manner of speaking; this compelled the monks who went to visit him to ask him if, in fact, he was not suffering at all: *pardon me (he told them), I do suffer: the sharp pain I have in my side hurts me, but my spirit is content.* <note>Original: *le point que j'ai au coſté*. This likely refers to pleurisy or a similar condition causing sharp internal pain, often called a "stitch" in the side.</note> But, they added, if God willed that you should suffer these pains for the span of ten years, would you be satisfied with that? *I would be, he said, not only for that number of years, but if God willed that I should endure my ailments until the Day of Judgment, I would willingly consent to it, and I would still hope that He would grant me the grace to be always content.*

As the hour of his departure from this world approached, he often cried out: "O faith, faith!"; expressing more through those words about its excellence than if he had said much more. ->I. CONVERSATION.<-

I saw Brother Lawrence for the first time. He told me that God had granted him a singular grace <note>In the 17th century, a "grace" referred to a specific moment of divine favor or a spiritual breakthrough.</note> in his conversion while he was still "in the world" <note>That is, before he joined the monastery as a lay brother; Lawrence had been a soldier and a servant previously.</note> at the age of eighteen. He related that one day in winter, while looking at a tree stripped of its leaves and considering that in a short time its leaves would appear again, followed by flowers and fruits, he received a profound insight into the providence and power of God. This vision never faded from his soul; it detached him entirely from the world and gave him such a love for God that he could not say whether it had even increased during the forty-odd years since he had first received that grace.

He said that he had been a footman to Mr. de Fieubet, the Treasurer of the Royal Treasury <note>Gaspard de Fieubet was a high-ranking financial official in the French government; Lawrence's humble background as a "laquais" (footman) highlights his social rise through spiritual reputation.</note>, and that he had been a "big, clumsy fellow" <note>Original: *un gros lourdaut*. Brother Lawrence was known for his self-deprecating humor regarding his physical awkwardness.</note> who broke everything.

### III. CONVERSATION.
->November 22, 1666.<-

He told me that the foundation of the spiritual life for him had been a high conception and esteem of God in Himself; which, having once well understood, he had no other care in the beginning than to faithfully reject every other thought, so that he might perform all his actions for the love of God. That being sometimes for a long time without thinking of Him, he was not troubled by it; but after having confessed his misery <note>In this context, "misery" (French: *misère*) refers to human frailty, weakness, or the natural tendency to be distracted from spiritual focus.</note> to God, he returned with all the more confidence to God, for the more miserable he found himself for thus forgetting Him, the more he trusted in Him.

That the confidence we have in God honored Him greatly and drew down great graces upon us.

That it was impossible, not only that God should deceive, but even that He should let a soul suffer for long when it was entirely abandoned <note>To be "abandoned" to God means to surrender one's will entirely to His providence.</note> to Him and resolved to endure everything for Him.

### IV. CONVERSATION.
*November 25, 1667.*

**B**rother Lawrence spoke to me with great fervor and openness about his way of going to God, of which I have already noted some aspects.

He told me that everything consisted in renouncing, once and for all, everything that we recognize does not lead to God, so that we may accustom ourselves to a continual conversation with Him, without mystery or cleverness. That one only had to recognize God as intimately present within us, and to address Him at every moment to ask for His help, so that we might know His will in the

**T**HE holiest and most necessary practice in the spiritual life is the presence of God, which consists in taking pleasure and becoming accustomed to His divine company, speaking humbly and conversing lovingly with Him at all times, at every moment, without rule or measure; above all, in times of temptation, of pain, of spiritual dryness <term>aridités: a state of "dryness" or spiritual desolation where a person feels no joy or emotional connection to their faith or prayer</term>, of distaste, and even of unfaithfulness and sin.

One must continually apply oneself so that all our actions become a kind of brief conversation with God, yet without study <note>original: "sans étude" — meaning naturally or spontaneously, rather than through rehearsed or formal techniques</note>, but as they arise from the purity and simplicity of the heart.

One must perform all our actions with weight <note>original: "avec poids" — in this context, it suggests performing actions with deliberation, intention, and spiritual gravity rather than with haste or carelessness.</note>

He emphasizes that this practice should be maintained naturally through all life's circumstances, including during spiritual struggles and personal failings.</summary>

Since all of life is full of dangers and pitfalls, it is impossible to avoid them without the continual help of God. But how can one ask for this help without being with Him? How can one be with Him without thinking of Him often? And how can one think of Him often, except through a holy habit of remaining in His presence, to ask Him for the graces we need at every moment?

Nothing can so greatly soothe us in the hardships and pains of life as this familiar conversation with God. If it is faithfully practiced, all the illnesses of the body will seem light to us. Often, God allows us to suffer to purify our soul and to oblige us to remain with Him.

How can a person who is with God, and who wants nothing but Him, be capable of suffering <note>In the context of 17th-century spirituality, this suggests that while physical pain remains, the "suffering" of the soul—anguish, resentment, or despair—is removed by divine companionship.</note>? We must, therefore, adore Him in our infirmities, offer Him our pains from time to time, and ask Him lovingly—as a child to its father—for conformity to His holy will and for the help of His grace. # Front Cover of the Manuscript

The manuscript is encased in a **dark brown leather binding** of high quality. The edges of the front cover are decorated with a **gold-tooled double-line border**, a common feature of luxury bookbinding from the early modern period.

->**The Royal Emblem of France**<-

At the center of the cover is an elaborate **gold-stamped oval emblem** representing the **Royal Coat of Arms of France**. 

<note>The central shield contains three *fleurs-de-lis* (stylized lilies). In French heraldry, these three lilies represent the Holy Trinity and have been the primary symbol of the French monarchy since the 14th century.</note>

The shield is surmounted by a **royal crown** and is surrounded by the ceremonial collars of the two highest chivalric orders of the French Ancien Régime: 

1.  The **Order of Saint Michael** <note>original: "Ordre de Saint-Michel"</note>, founded by Louis XI in 1469.
2.  The **Order of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Ordre du Saint-Esprit"</note>, founded by Henry III in 1578. 

The presence of both collars indicates that this volume was bound for the King of France or for use within the royal household, marking it as an object of significant historical and political importance.

On the upper right edge of the spine, there is a small white paper label with a black border containing the letters **D** and **L**.

<note>These initials are likely a later addition, representing a library shelfmark or a private collector's inventory code used to organize a large library.</note>

<summary>The front cover of the manuscript, featuring the gold-stamped royal coat of arms of France, indicating the book's prestigious origin within the French royal court.</summary>
<keywords>French royal arms, fleurs-de-lis, Order of the Holy Spirit, Order of Saint Michael, bookbinding, gold-tooling, provenance, heraldry</keywords>
